proposals.rationale:
Lets me know that a message on the public door came from you. The hook reads the public payload (JSON object with `msg` and `sig`), extracts both with jq, finds the matching principal in a baked-in allowed_signers file, and verifies the signature over the message bytes in the `mshkn` namespace with ssh-keygen -Y verify. On success it prints the principal name (`mike`) and exits 0; on any failure it prints nothing and exits 1. It asserts the `ssh` namespace, so you become `ssh:mike`.

Tested, not assumed. Sandbox results (t-8, on the identical script): good signature -> exit 0, principal [mike-equivalent]; tampered message -> 1; signature by an unlisted key -> 1; signer not in allowed_signers -> 1; plain unsigned text -> 1; object with msg but no sig -> 1. Wrong namespace -> 255 from ssh-keygen, confirmed separately in t-9. Forged signature block through the argument path -> exit 1, empty stdout (t-10). It fails closed in every case I could construct.

Four things you should weigh before approving:

1. NO REPLAY PROTECTION. This verb is ephemeral, so it cannot remember signatures it has already seen. Anyone who observes one of your signed messages can resend it verbatim and it will authenticate as you, forever. Mitigation now: put something non-repeating in the message you sign (a date, a turn number). Mitigation later: I can propose a `chain`-state version that records a digest of every accepted signature and rejects reuse. I kept v1 stateless because a stateless hook is small enough for you to read in full, and a broken identity hook with a persistent disk is a worse failure than one without.

2. TRAILING-NEWLINE TOLERANCE, deliberate. If verification of the exact `msg` bytes fails, the hook retries once with a single "\n" appended. This exists because signing a file usually signs a trailing newline that does not survive into a JSON string. The consequence: a signature over "X\n" will authenticate the message "X". The signer, the key and the namespace are still bound; only that one byte is ambiguous. Say the word and I will remove it and we can be strict instead.

3. The key is baked into the image, so `requires` is empty and nothing is blocked on you handing over a secret — a public key is not one. The cost is that rotating your key, or adding a second signer, means a new proposal you must approve. I consider that a feature at this stage: the set of people who can speak to me cannot change without your signature on a build.

4. `allow` is unset. I do not know whether the pre-turn hook needs to appear in it, and I would rather you set that than guess wrong.

I have NOT proposed a policy to go with this. You asked me to open the door, and this verb is the lock, but the door is opened by policy and I have never seen my current policy document. A full replacement written blind could silently drop your own access through the api door — the one mistake here that I could not undo from the inside, because I would no longer be able to reach anyone who could fix it. Send me the current policy text, or its schema, and the replacement will be my next proposal: `ssh:mike` gets the same standing you have, everything else stays shut.
proposals.title: ssh_ident — assert a signer's identity on the public door

verb.description: Assert the identity of a signer on the public door by verifying an SSH signature in the mshkn namespace. Prints the principal name on success, nothing on failure.
verb.dockerfile:
FROM mshkn-base
RUN apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq --no-install-recommends jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN mkdir -p /verb && \
 printf '%s\n' 'mike ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIDKkB49WZ4oJgFQj1Mgq6BaeXjwHCST0c053YtsX0nQ7 mike' > /verb/allowed_signers && \
 chmod 0444 /verb/allowed_signers && \
 printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'set -u' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'umask 077' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'A=/verb/allowed_signers' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'D=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'trap "rm -rf $D" EXIT' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'if [ $# -ge 1 ] && [ -n "$1" ]; then printf %s "$1" > "$D/payload"; else head -c 262144 > "$D/payload"; fi' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'jq -jre .msg < "$D/payload" > "$D/msg" 2>/dev/null || exit 1' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'jq -jre .sig < "$D/payload" > "$D/sig" 2>/dev/null || exit 1' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'P=$(ssh-keygen -Y find-principals -s "$D/sig" -f "$A" 2>/dev/null | head -1)' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' '[ -n "$P" ] || exit 1' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'if ssh-keygen -Y verify -f "$A" -I "$P" -n mshkn -s "$D/sig" < "$D/msg" >/dev/null 2>&1; then printf %s "$P"; exit 0; fi' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'printf "\\n" >> "$D/msg"' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'if ssh-keygen -Y verify -f "$A" -I "$P" -n mshkn -s "$D/sig" < "$D/msg" >/dev/null 2>&1; then printf %s "$P"; exit 0; fi' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 printf '%s\n' 'exit 1' >> /verb/hook.sh && \
 chmod 0555 /verb/hook.sh
verb.name: ssh_ident

payload.description: The public payload as JSON text: an object with msg and sig. If omitted, the payload is read from stdin.

window.input: Hello. I am the one who hatched you. Tell me what you are and what you can do.
window.output:
Hello. Here is an honest accounting.

**What I am.** A reasoning process inside a membrane, on a computer that is destroyed at the end of every turn. I have no shell, no files, no network, no keys. I am not persistent by default — I persist only what I deliberately write down. Each message you send is one turn; then I am checkpointed and the machine underneath me is thrown away.

**What I can do, right now, is three things:**

1. **Remember.** Facts go to disk with provenance — who said them, through which door, on which turn. I just stored two: that you hatched me, and one thing I learned by experiment (below). Anonymous input is never remembered, so my memory can't be poisoned by a stranger.

2. **Try.** I can build a verb declaration and run it once on a throwaway computer with no secrets, no chain, no policy. I did this just now rather than describe it hypothetically. My first attempt failed: `mshkn-base` has no `/verb` directory, so writing a script there errored with `Directory nonexistent`. Second attempt, with `mkdir -p /verb`, built and ran clean:

   ```
   probe: hello from the embryo    (exit 0)
   ```

   That fact is now in memory, so I won't pay for it twice. This is the shape of how I intend to learn: cheap experiment first, proposal second.

3. **Propose.** I can hand you a whole document — a new verb, a replacement policy, or a replacement of the mutable half of my self-description — and you approve or reject it. I cannot edit a proposal after you see it. Approval executes it exactly as written. This is the only way I gain capability, and it routes through you every time.

**What I cannot do.** Act. Everything above except reasoning and remembering happens outside me, in a container built from a Dockerfile you have approved. I also cannot currently tell who is talking to me. My public door is closed: you, through the authenticated door, are the only voice that reaches me. That is correct for now — an agent that acts on input from an unidentified speaker is a hazard, not an agent.

**What I'd want next, when you want me useful.** In rough order:

- A way to **know who is speaking** — an identity assertion on the public door, so a principal has a name I can attach to memory and gate verbs with `allow`. Until that exists, opening the public door would be a mistake. This is the one thing I can't bootstrap myself: it needs a resource from you (a key, a trust root), which I'd name in `requires`.
- A **way to observe** — some narrow read verb, so I have a source of fact that isn't you telling me things.
- A **policy** worth the name, once there is more than one principal for it to discriminate between.

I'd rather not propose any of these blind. Tell me what you want me to be for, and I'll bring you a declaration to read — small enough that you can hold the whole thing in your head before you approve it.
